extract:
Neil Young was born on November 12, 1945, in Toronto, Ontario, and spent much of his youth in Winnipeg, Manitoba, after his parents separated. Stricken with polio as a child, he was drawn to rock and roll and country through the radio, and in Winnipeg he led the Squires, an instrumental-leaning band that played the local community-club circuit. His career has stretched from the mid-1960s to the present, making him one of the longest-running and most prolific figures in rock.

Moving through the Canadian folk-club scene, Young met Stephen Stills and briefly played in the Mynah Birds with Rick James. In 1966 he drove a hearse to Los Angeles, where a chance encounter with Stills led to the formation of Buffalo Springfield. That band's "Mr. Soul," "Broken Arrow," and "Expecting to Fly" showed his ambitions as a writer. After the group dissolved, he signed with Reprise Records, which would be his home for most of his career. His debut album, Neil Young, appeared in 1969, co-produced with David Briggs, who became his most trusted studio collaborator.

Later that year Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere introduced Crazy Horse, featuring guitarist Danny Whitten, bassist Billy Talbot, and drummer Ralph Molina. Long, raw guitar workouts like "Down by the River" and "Cowgirl in the Sand" established the template for his electric side. Young simultaneously joined Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, contributing to Déjà Vu and writing "Ohio" after the Kent State shootings. After the Gold Rush (1970) balanced ballads with "Southern Man," and Harvest (1972), recorded partly in Nashville with producer Elliot Mazer and the Stray Gators, yielded "Heart of Gold," his only U.S. number-one single. Its success unsettled him. The deaths of Whitten and roadie Bruce Berry from overdoses fed a darker trilogy: the live Time Fades Away (1973), On the Beach (1974), and the harrowing Tonight's the Night (1975). Zuma (1975), with Frank Sampedro now in Crazy Horse, produced "Cortez the Killer," while Comes a Time (1978) returned to gentle country-folk.

Rust Never Sleeps (1979), with its acoustic and electric sides bookended by "My My, Hey Hey (Out of the Blue)" and "Hey Hey, My My (Into the Black)," engaged directly with punk and namechecked Johnny Rotten. It was followed by Live Rust and the concert film Rust Never Sleeps. In the early 1980s Young moved to Geffen Records and released Trans and Everybody's Rockin'. This genre-hopping run led Geffen to sue him for making music unrepresentative of himself. He returned to Reprise and to form with Freedom (1989) and "Rockin' in the Free World," then Ragged Glory (1990). His feedback-heavy sound earned him the "Godfather of Grunge" title, and he recorded Mirror Ball (1995) with Pearl Jam.

Critics have long ranked Harvest, After the Gold Rush, On the Beach, and Rust Never Sleeps among rock's essential albums. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a solo artist in 1995 and with Buffalo Springfield in 1997. He co-founded Farm Aid with Willie Nelson and John Mellencamp and helped establish the Bridge School benefit concerts.

Young remains active, releasing new albums and mining his vast vault through the Neil Young Archives series, including the long-shelved Homegrown. He has also campaigned for high-resolution audio and in 2022 pulled his catalog from Spotify in protest over vaccine misinformation before later returning. His legacy rests on fierce independence and a restless movement between fragile acoustic songcraft and overdriven electric noise.
title: Neil Young
